audits.mathematicalReason: The enclosing rectangle has width 2·6 + 3·1 = 15 feet and height 3·2 + 4·1 = 10 feet. Its area is 150 square feet. The six beds occupy 6·6·2 = 72 square feet, so the walkways occupy 150 − 72 = 78 square feet. This directly supports composite-area subtraction, with rectangle-area calculation as support.

figureEvidence.fact: The six beds form three aligned rows and two columns, with their 6-foot sides horizontal and 2-foot sides vertical. The separating and surrounding walkway widths are all labeled 1 foot.

audits.mathematicalReason: A cube's twelve edges form three parallel-direction classes, each containing four edges. Each class contributes C(4,2) = 6 unordered pairs, giving 3·6 = 18 pairs. Classifying parallel lines in space and choosing unordered pairs are both defensible assessed scopes for this method; a combination formula is not the only possible counting method.

figureEvidence.fact: The labeled cube has parallel edge classes {AB, CD, EF, GH}, {AE, BF, CG, DH}, and {AD, BC, EH, FG}. Each class contains four distinct edges.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let the regular octagon's side length, also the center square's side length, be s > 0. Completing the octagon to an enclosing square adds four isosceles right triangles. Each has hypotenuse s and legs s/√2, so the enclosing square has side (1 + √2)s and the four removed triangles have total area s². Thus the octagon's area is [(1 + √2)² − 1]s² = 2(1 + √2)s². Uniform landing probability gives s²/[2(1 + √2)s²] = (√2 − 1)/2. The proposed geometry scopes fit this calculation, but the continuous area-to-probability step remains unmapped by the supplied definitions.

needsNewNodes: Provisionally: uniform planar geometric probability, P(subregion) = area(subregion)/area(sample region), if scope lookup confirms that no existing probability node covers it.

figureEvidence.fact: The interior vertical and horizontal segments extend through endpoints of the octagon's axis-parallel sides, forming the center square. Consequently, its side length equals an octagon side length. Together with the stated regularity, the four corner cuts are isosceles right triangles.

audits.mathematicalReason: The ball has radius 2 inches. On the two troughs, internal tangency makes the center-path radii 100 − 2 = 98 and 80 − 2 = 78 inches. On the crest, external tangency makes the radius 60 + 2 = 62 inches. These paths are semicircles that meet at their corresponding endpoints, so the total center-path length is π(98 + 62 + 78) = 238π inches. The no-slip condition concerns rotation and introduces no additional center-path distance.

figureEvidence.fact: From A to B, the track consists of a lower semicircular trough labeled R1, an upper semicircular crest labeled R2, and a lower semicircular trough labeled R3. The arcs join along their common diameter line, and the ball travels on the upper side of the track.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let the bottom and top radii be R > r > 0, the sphere radius be ρ, and the frustum height be h = 2ρ. In an axial section, equal tangent lengths in the tangential isosceles trapezoid give slant length L = R + r. Pythagoras gives (R + r)² = (R − r)² + h², hence ρ² = Rr. Subtracting similar cone volumes gives Vfrustum = πh(R² + Rr + r²)/3. Using Vsphere = 4πρ³/3 and Vfrustum = 2Vsphere yields R² + Rr + r² = 4ρ² = 4Rr. Therefore x = R/r satisfies x² − 3x + 1 = 0. Since x > 1, x = (3 + √5)/2. The listed support scopes fit this derivation, but coverage of the sphere-volume step cannot be settled from the supplied definitions.

needsNewNodes: Conditional only: absolute sphere volume V = (4/3)πρ³ and its use in volume comparisons, if lookup of cnm_h112 and, if necessary, cnm_h111 confirms that neither covers it.
limitations: The mathematical answer is resolved, but the full assessed scope remains unresolved.
Request scope lookup for cnm_h112, titled 'Volume and surface area of a sphere'; cnm_h111 may also merit lookup. Neither coverage nor exclusion should be inferred solely from these titles.

figureEvidence.fact: The depicted frustum has a larger bottom base and a smaller top base, with an inscribed sphere. Combining this with the stated right-circular geometry gives an axial isosceles trapezoid whose incircle is tangent to both bases and both sloping sides.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let M be the midpoint of AB and the common tangency point of circles A and B. Tangency of circle C to line AB at M places its center one unit perpendicular to AB. Set A = (−1,0), B = (1,0), and C = (0,1). Circles A and C intersect at M = (0,0) and P = (−1,1); A, M, C, P form a unit square. Their overlap lens consists of two quarter-circle sectors minus that square, so its area is π/2 − 1. The overlap with circle B has the same area, and the two lenses have no positive-area intersection. The requested area is π − 2(π/2 − 1) = 2.
candidateFindings: v01: The sole assessed node cnm_p150 has an explicit triangle/rectangle decomposition criterion, whereas the stated method evaluates circular-sector overlaps. cnm_257 explicitly covers sector areas and irregular-region areas and should be assessed rather than merely support this method.

figureEvidence.fact: The figure places C above the midpoint of the centers A and B, with circle C passing through their common tangency point. The shaded region is inside C with both overlap lenses excluded. This supports interpreting the stated tangency as tangency of circle C to line AB at its midpoint.

audits.mathematicalReason: The outer square has side 2 and area 4. The inner square joins the outer square's side midpoints, so the four corner triangles each have perpendicular legs 1 and area 1/2; the inner square therefore has area 4 − 4(1/2) = 2. The shaded portion inside the circle has area π − 2, while the entire shaded region between the squares has area 4 − 2 = 2. Their ratio is (π − 2)/2 ≈ 0.5708, closest to 1/2. Here cnm_p150 is justified by the polygonal four-triangle decomposition, without needing to extend its scope to arbitrary curved figures.

figureEvidence.fact: The inner square's vertices coincide with the circle's tangency points at the outer square's side midpoints. The inner square is unshaded, and all of the outer square outside it is shaded, including both the circular segments and the regions outside the circle.
